title: War Dept Waives Secrecy Rules for UAP Disclosures
excerpt: War Dept Waives Secrecy Rules for UAP Disclosures
content:
The Department of War on Tuesday announced a new legal waiver allowing current and former government personnel and contractors to provide protected information about unidentified anomalous phenomena to officials leading the Trump administration's UAP disclosure effort.

The waiver establishes a "legally protected disclosure mechanism" for people with access to UAP-related National Defense Information to speak directly with representatives of the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters, or PURSUE, according to the department.

The department said the waiver overrides civil and administrative enforcement provisions in nondisclosure agreements and Special Access Program Indoctrination Agreements — but only for disclosures made to the PURSUE team.

"This targeted legal relief establishes an authorized pipeline for systematic review, security evaluation, and potential declassification of historical and ongoing UAP data," the department said.

Officials said some people with direct knowledge of UAP-related programs have historically cited fears of legal liability, losing security clearances, or facing administrative action for discussing information covered by secrecy agreements.

The new waiver is intended to remove those obstacles without broadly releasing classified information.

The action represents the latest step in the Trump administration's gradual effort to disclose more of what the federal government knows about UAPs, commonly known as UFOs. Trump directed agencies in February to identify and release government records concerning UAPs, UFOs, and possible extraterrestrial life.

The government says that effort requires searching and reviewing tens of millions of records held across numerous agencies.

Since May, the administration has released five tranches of material through PURSUE, including historical records, photographs, and videos.

The fifth batch was published Aug. 7, following earlier releases beginning May 8.

The releases have included intriguing unresolved sightings, including reports involving glowing orbs, unusual discs, and other unexplained objects, but have thus far produced no definitive public evidence establishing an extraterrestrial origin for UAPs.

Nor have the documents proven long-standing claims that the government possesses alien spacecraft or technology.

The department itself cautions that records placed in the PURSUE archive are classified as unresolved because the government lacks enough information to make a definitive determination about what was observed.

Tuesday's waiver could ultimately prove more consequential than another document release by potentially allowing people with knowledge of previously restricted programs to provide information for government review and possible declassification.

However tantalizing the idea of offering protection to whistleblowers, what that process will eventually bring into public view remains unclear.
